title: A parametric and a polar curve: what path does it trace, and which way?
summary: A curve given by x(t), y(t) or by r(theta) is drawn as a path in the plane. Equal axis scales keep shapes honest and colour along the path tells you the direction of travel.

media.alt: Left: an outward spiral from the origin coloured from purple to yellow with an arrow showing counter-clockwise travel. Right: a rose curve with three large and three small petals, coloured by angle, with a colour bar.
media.caption: Reference render of class F1.3 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data. Standard theory only.

read_the_figure.question: What path does it trace?
read_the_figure.axes: Both panels plot the plane: horizontal x, vertical y, with equal scale per unit on both axes. Left: x(t) = t cos t / 4, y(t) = t sin t / 4. Right: x = r cos(theta), y = r sin(theta) with r = cos 3 theta + 0.3. Colour is the parameter, 0 to 4 pi, with one colour bar.
look_at: Where does the path start (amber dot) and which way does it go (arrow, then dark to light colour)?
Does the path cross itself? The rose does, at the origin; the spiral never does.
Are loops round? With equal axis scales, a circle looks like a circle, so lengths and angles can be trusted.
Why does the rose have six lobes when cos 3 theta suggests three? Look at the sign of r.
as_drawn: Both panels use equal aspect. The colour bar belongs to both and reads 'parameter t or theta'.
The spiral runs counter-clockwise from the origin to (3.14, 0). The rose starts at (1.3, 0) and ends there.
The three small lobes are traced where r is negative; they are plotted on the opposite side of the origin.
read_the_figure.proves: The shape of the path and its direction. It does not show speed: the same path can be traversed fast or slowly, and the colour only gives the order, not equal-time spacing.
if_wrong: Unequal axis scales: circles become ellipses and angles lie.
A path that overlaps itself with one constant colour: you cannot tell the direction or the order of loops.
A polar plot where r is negative but treated as positive: lobes appear in the wrong place.

terms.meaning: A running variable (time, angle, arc length) that orders the points of a curve.
A curve given as a pair of functions of one parameter.
A curve given by a distance from the origin as a function of angle.
One unit along x is drawn as long as one unit along y.
The order in which the parameter visits the points; shown by an arrow or a colour ramp.
The distance along the path, which is generally not the parameter.

remember: Polar to Cartesian: x = r cos(theta), y = r sin(theta); a negative r points the opposite way.
Equal aspect or the shape is a lie.
Colour = parameter shows direction; it does not show speed.
Arc length: L = integral of the speed, sqrt(x'^2 + y'^2) dt.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Each point on the path is a pair (x, y) in the plane, so position encodes the curve itself. Colour encodes the parameter, which is not an axis. An arrow gives the sense of travel locally; the amber dot marks where the parameter starts.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: The question is geometric (a shape in the plane), but the data are functions of a hidden parameter. Plotting x against y removes the parameter from the axes and shows the path directly. Colour restores the information that was removed: where the path was first and where it is later. Equal axis scales keep distances, angles and curvature meaningful.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: If the axes are not equal, a circle becomes an ellipse and a right angle looks acute. Colour shows order but not speed: equal colour steps are equal parameter steps, not equal distances. A path that retraces itself hides the earlier pass. A polar curve with negative r is easy to misread, as the six lobes of the rose show.

understand.title: Why each required item matters
understand.text: Equal aspect makes the picture a faithful map. Direction colouring answers 'which way?', which the shape alone cannot. Together they let you read curvature, loops and winding directly.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: For speed, plot x(t) and y(t) as time series or put tick marks at equal time intervals along the path. For many loops, animate the point. For curvature, colour the line by curvature (see F3.6). For a plain function of x, the ordinary curve (F1.1) is simpler.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Put a dot every 0.5 in the parameter along both curves: the spacing of the dots shows the speed, which the colour ramp hides. Draw the spiral's arc-length labels at each full turn.

steps.title: From polar to the plane
steps.note: With r = cos 3 theta + 0.3 the radius is negative where cos 3 theta < -0.3, which happens for three angle intervals in [0, 2 pi]: six sign changes of r in all, hence three small inner loops between three big petals. r runs from -0.7 to 1.3.

steps.title: Speed and arc length of the spiral
steps.note: For x = t cos t / 4 and y = t sin t / 4 the speed is sqrt(1 + t^2) / 4. The closed form 20.2048 agrees with a numerical sum of the plotted points.

steps.title: Same path, different clock
steps.note: A path does not determine its parameterisation. This is why colour is a convenience, not a speed gauge.

worked.title: Reading the reference render
worked.problem: From the figure: (1) which way does the spiral go and where does it end? (2) How many lobes does the rose have and why? (3) How far apart are successive turns of the spiral on the positive x axis?

solution.text: The arrow points counter-clockwise and the colour darkens toward the start at the origin; the yellow end sits at about (3.14, 0).
Six lobes: three large ones where r > 0 and three small ones where r < 0 (r ranges from -0.7 to 1.3).
The spiral crosses the positive x axis at t = 2 pi (x about 1.57) and t = 4 pi (x about 3.14), so turns are 1.57 apart: an Archimedean spiral.

worked.answer: Counter-clockwise, ending at (3.14, 0); six lobes because r changes sign; evenly spaced turns 1.57 apart.

analyze.q: If the horizontal axis were stretched by a factor of two, what would the spiral turns look like and what would you wrongly conclude?
The rose plotted with r = |cos 3 theta + 0.3| instead. Which lobes change?
analyze.hint: Absolute value flips the negative-r parts to the other side.

analyze.q: How would you show the speed on the spiral?

evaluate.q: Two people plot the same curve with different parameterisations and get the same picture but different colour patterns. Is one wrong?
evaluate.hint: A path and a parameterisation are different objects.

create: Plot the cardioid r = 1 + sin(theta) and the astroid x = cos^3 t, y = sin^3 t with equal aspect, a direction arrow and dots at equal time steps.
Make the colour ramp map arc length instead of parameter and compare how the two look.

checks.q: Why must the axes have equal scale in this kind of plot?
checks.hint: What happens to a circle otherwise?
checks.answer: The plot shows geometry. Unequal scales distort lengths and angles, so shapes, loops and curvature would be misread.

checks.q: The spiral's speed is sqrt(1 + t^2)/4. At t = 4 pi, how fast is the point moving per unit of t?
checks.answer: sqrt(1 + 157.9)/4 = 3.15 units per unit t: the point moves faster the farther out it is.

checks.q: Two lobes of the rose are the same size but one is traced by r > 0 and the other by r < 0. How would you tell which is which on the figure?
checks.hint: Use the colour ramp and the sign of r.
checks.answer: Follow the colour ramp: the small inner lobes occur where cos 3 theta < -0.3, at theta in about 0.63 to 1.46 etc.; for those angles the point is drawn on the opposite side of the origin.
